subChunks.title: The Periodic Table & Chemical Bonding

storyBeats.txt: Dmitri Mendeleev was not the first chemist to notice patterns in the elements, Theodora said. But he was the one who trusted the pattern enough to leave gaps — gaps where undiscovered elements should be. Three were found within his lifetime, with properties matching his predictions almost exactly. That is what a good periodic table does: it predicts.

The modern periodic table is not a list. It is a map of electronic structure. An element's position tells you almost everything about how it will behave: how many electrons it will gain or lose, what bonds it will form, whether it is a metal or non-metal, how reactive it is.

And bonds — the connections between atoms — are what make chemistry possible at all. Without bonds, matter would be a cloud of isolated atoms. Bonds are what make water wet, salt crystalline, and DNA capable of encoding information.

subChunks.hookHtml: The periodic table is one of the greatest intellectual achievements in the history of science: a single two-dimensional arrangement that encodes the electronic structure of all 118 known elements and predicts their chemical behaviour. Understanding the periodic table means understanding not just what elements exist, but why they behave as they do — and how the way atoms bond together produces the astonishing variety of materials in the universe.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Atomic Structure Review

An atom consists of a nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by electrons. The atomic number (Z) = number of protons = defines the element. The mass number = protons + neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different neutron numbers (e.g., ¹²C and ¹⁴C).

Electrons occupy energy levels (shells) and subshells (s, p, d, f). The first shell holds 2 electrons; the second holds 8. The arrangement of electrons in these shells (the electron configuration) determines an element's chemical properties. The outermost electrons (valence electrons) are the ones that participate in bonding.

Organisation of the Periodic Table

Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. The table's structure reflects electron configuration:

  • Periods (rows): Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells. Period 2 elements have 2 shells; Period 3 have 3 shells.
  • Groups (columns): Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties. Group 1 (alkali metals) all have 1 valence electron and are highly reactive. Group 17 (halogens) all have 7 valence electrons and readily form −1 ions. Group 18 (noble gases) have full outer shells and are largely unreactive.

Periodic Trends

Several properties follow predictable patterns across the table:

  • Atomic radius: Decreases left to right across a period (increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer). Increases down a group (additional electron shells increase radius).
  • Ionisation energy: Energy to remove an electron. Increases across a period; decreases down a group. Noble gases have highest ionisation energies.
  • Electronegativity: Tendency to attract electrons in a bond (Pauling scale). Fluorine is most electronegative (3.98). Increases across a period; decreases down a group. Metals have low electronegativity; non-metals have high.
  • Metallic character: Metals (left/centre of table) lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals (right) gain electrons to form negative ions; metalloids (borderline) have intermediate properties.

Ionic Bonding

Occurs between metals and non-metals. The metal loses electrons to form a positive ion (cation); the non-metal gains electrons to form a negative ion (anion). Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions forms an ionic lattice.

Properties of ionic compounds: high melting points (strong lattice forces); conduct electricity when dissolved in water or molten (ions free to move); soluble in water (water molecules surround and separate ions); brittle (layers shift and like charges repel).

Example: NaCl — Na loses 1 electron to become Na⁺; Cl gains 1 electron to become Cl⁻. Attraction forms the salt crystal lattice.

Covalent Bonding

Occurs between non-metals. Atoms share electron pairs, each shared pair constituting one bond. A single bond shares 1 pair (e.g., H–H, H–Cl); a double bond shares 2 pairs (C=O in CO₂); a triple bond shares 3 pairs (N≡N in N₂).

Properties of covalent substances: small molecules have low melting/boiling points (weak forces between molecules, strong bonds within); giant covalent structures (diamond, SiO₂) have very high melting points; most do not conduct electricity (no charged particles free to move).

Electronegativity difference determines polarity: if one atom in a covalent bond is more electronegative, the shared electrons are pulled toward it, creating a polar bond (δ+ on one end, δ− on the other). Water (H₂O) has a bent structure and polar bonds — making it an excellent polar solvent. The polarity of water is central to biology, chemistry, and geology.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, valence electrons are delocalised — they flow freely through the lattice of positive metal ions. This electron sea explains: high electrical conductivity (electrons carry current); high thermal conductivity (electrons transfer kinetic energy); malleability and ductility (layers of ions slide without breaking the electron sea); metallic lustre (free electrons reflect light).

Intermolecular Forces

Between molecules (as opposed to within them): van der Waals forces (all molecules) — weak temporary dipole interactions; permanent dipole-dipole forces (polar molecules); hydrogen bonds — strong intermolecular attraction between H bonded to F, O, or N and a lone pair on another F, O, or N. Hydrogen bonding is why water has anomalously high boiling point, why ice is less dense than liquid water (unusual), and how DNA double helix base pairs hold together.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why water dissolves salt but oil does not — using the concept of polarity and like-dissolves-like.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Carbon (Z=6) can form four bonds and produces two important structures: diamond and graphite. (1) Describe the bonding in diamond — what type of bond, how many per carbon atom, and what does this predict about its properties? (2) In graphite, each carbon bonds to three others in flat sheets. The fourth electron per carbon is delocalised across each sheet. What bonding type is this, and what properties does it predict? (3) Why is graphite a conductor of electricity but diamond is not? (4) Carbon also forms CO₂. Draw (describe) the bonding in CO₂ and explain whether this molecule is polar overall, given that C–O bonds are polar.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Diamond: each carbon forms four covalent bonds to four neighbouring carbons in a giant tetrahedral lattice — a giant covalent structure. Predictions: extremely high melting point (very strong, extensive covalent network throughout); hardest natural material (no planes of weakness — all bonds in 3D); does not conduct electricity (no free electrons or ions); transparent (large band gap).

(2) Graphite: three covalent bonds per carbon in hexagonal flat sheets — also giant covalent. The delocalised electrons form a system analogous to metallic bonding within each sheet (a pi-electron system). Predictions: conducts electricity (delocalised electrons within sheets); slippery/lubricant (sheets slide over each other; weak van der Waals forces between sheets but strong covalent bonds within); grey/black lustre (delocalised electrons absorb and re-emit light); flaky/soft (sheets cleave apart easily — why pencils write by leaving graphite layers on paper).

(3) Graphite conducts because each carbon contributes one delocalised electron to the pi system within each layer — these electrons can move under an electric field. Diamond has all four carbon electrons fixed in localised covalent bonds with no free electrons — it cannot conduct electricity.

(4) CO₂ structure: O=C=O. Two C=O double bonds, linear arrangement. Each C=O bond is polar (oxygen is more electronegative, drawing electron density toward it — each oxygen is δ−, the carbon between them is δ+). However, CO₂ is linear — the two polar bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel each other out. The result is a non-polar molecule overall. This is why CO₂ is a gas at room temperature (non-polar molecules have only weak van der Waals forces between them) and why it does not dissolve readily in non-polar solvents but also dissolves in water (the water molecules can induce temporary dipoles).
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Sodium chloride (NaCl) melts at 801°C and conducts electricity when dissolved in water. Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) boils at 78°C and does not conduct electricity in any state. Polyethylene (a long-chain covalent polymer) melts around 130°C and does not conduct. Copper melts at 1,085°C and conducts electricity as a solid. For each compound, identify the type(s) of bonding present and explain why each property (melting/boiling point and conductivity) follows from the bonding type.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
NaCl — ionic bonding. Melting point 801°C: ionic lattices have strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in a regular three-dimensional arrangement; considerable energy is required to overcome these forces and separate the ions — hence high melting point. Does not conduct as solid (ions fixed in lattice positions); conducts when dissolved or molten because ions are free to move and carry charge.

Ethanol — covalent bonding within molecules, with hydrogen bonding between molecules. Boiling point 78°C: ethanol is a small covalent molecule; individual molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds (O–H group) and van der Waals forces — relatively weak intermolecular forces compared to ionic or metallic forces, hence low boiling point. Does not conduct: no ions or free electrons in any state; ethanol molecules carry no charge and have no mobile charge carriers.

Polyethylene — giant covalent structure (polymer). Melting point 130°C: the polymer chains are long but each chain is held to others only by van der Waals forces (not covalent bonds between chains) — moderate melting point. Within each chain, covalent C–C bonds are very strong but are not broken on melting; the polymer softens as chains slide past each other. Does not conduct: all electrons are localised in covalent bonds; no free electrons or ions.

Copper — metallic bonding. Melting point 1,085°C: metallic bonds (electrostatic attraction between delocalised electrons and positive metal ion lattice) are strong — high melting point comparable to ionic solids. Conducts electricity as solid: delocalised electrons are free to flow through the lattice under a potential difference — copper is an excellent conductor. Malleable: layers of ions can slide past each other without disrupting the delocalised electron sea.
learningObjectives: Explain the organisation of the periodic table in terms of periods, groups, and electron configuration, with examples of periodic trends.
Describe ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding, including the types of particles and forces involved in each.
Predict properties (melting point, conductivity, solubility) from the bonding type of a given substance.
Explain polarity in covalent bonds and molecules, and describe how hydrogen bonding arises and why it matters for water and biological molecules.
commonMistakes: Confusing bond polarity with molecular polarity — CO₂ has polar C=O bonds but is non-polar overall because the bond dipoles cancel in its linear, symmetrical structure.
Stating that ionic compounds conduct electricity as solids — they do not; the ions are fixed in the lattice and only become free to conduct when dissolved or molten.
Mixing up atomic radius trend direction — radius decreases left to right across a period (more protons attract electrons closer) and increases down a group (more electron shells).
Thinking hydrogen bonds are bonds within a molecule — hydrogen bonds are intermolecular (or intramolecular in some proteins/DNA) forces between different molecules, not the covalent O–H bond itself.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly identifies bonding type from the elements involved (metal+non-metal → ionic; non-metal+non-metal → covalent; metal → metallic) and explains each type.
Accurately predicts properties (melting point, conductivity) from bonding type with correct mechanistic explanation.
Explains periodic trends in atomic radius and electronegativity with reference to nuclear charge and electron shells.
Correctly assesses molecular polarity by considering both bond polarity and molecular geometry.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A dimensionless measure of an atom's tendency to attract shared electrons in a bond — fluorine (3.98) is highest; francium and caesium (~0.7) are lowest; differences >1.7 typically indicate ionic character.

A strong intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to F, O, or N and a lone electron pair on another F, O, or N atom — responsible for water's high boiling point, ice's lower density than liquid water, and DNA base pairing.

Different structural forms of the same element — e.g., diamond and graphite (both carbon); O₂ and O₃ (ozone); white and red phosphorus. Allotropes have different properties due to different bonding arrangements.
The energy released when gaseous ions combine to form an ionic lattice — a measure of ionic bond strength; larger for ions with higher charge and smaller radius (NaF vs CsI).

Published in 1869, Mendeleev's table arranged elements by atomic weight and left gaps for undiscovered elements — eka-aluminium (gallium, found 1875) and eka-silicon (germanium, found 1886) matched his predictions almost exactly.

questions.questionHtml: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar chemical properties because they:
options: Have the same number of electron shells (same period)
Have the same number of valence (outer shell) electrons
Have the same number of neutrons
questions.correctAnswer: Have the same number of valence (outer shell) electrons
questions.explanationHtml: Chemical properties are determined primarily by valence electrons — the electrons available for bonding. Elements in the same group (vertical column) all have the same number of valence electrons, so they form similar types of bonds and ions. For example, all Group 1 elements have 1 valence electron and tend to form +1 ions. The number of electron shells (periods) and atomic mass increase down a group.

questions.questionHtml: Magnesium oxide (MgO) has a melting point of 2,852°C. Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) melts at −75.5°C. Which statement best explains this enormous difference in melting points?
options: Magnesium oxide has more atoms per molecule than sulfur dioxide
MgO is ionic with strong electrostatic lattice forces requiring large energy to overcome; SO₂ is a small covalent molecule with only weak van der Waals intermolecular forces
Sulfur dioxide is a gas at room temperature because it contains sulfur, which is unstable
Magnesium is a heavier metal, so its compound has a higher melting point
questions.correctAnswer: MgO is ionic with strong electrostatic lattice forces requiring large energy to overcome; SO₂ is a small covalent molecule with only weak van der Waals intermolecular forces
questions.explanationHtml: MgO forms a giant ionic lattice: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions held by strong electrostatic forces; very high energy is needed to disrupt the lattice. SO₂ is a covalent molecule: within SO₂, S=O bonds are strong covalent bonds, but between SO₂ molecules, only weak van der Waals and dipole-dipole forces exist. Breaking these intermolecular forces requires little energy — hence the very low melting point. This difference reflects bonding type, not atom size or mass.

questions.questionHtml: A student argues: "Water (H₂O) should boil at a lower temperature than hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) because oxygen is lighter than sulfur — lighter molecules should be more volatile." Why is this argument incorrect?
options: The argument is correct — water does boil lower than H₂S

The argument ignores hydrogen bonding: O is small and highly electronegative, enabling strong H-bonds between water molecules that require much more energy to break than the weaker van der Waals forces between H₂S molecules
The argument ignores that H₂S has more electrons and therefore stronger van der Waals forces than H₂O
The argument is incorrect because mass determines boiling point — heavier molecules always boil higher
questions.correctAnswer: The argument ignores hydrogen bonding: O is small and highly electronegative, enabling strong H-bonds between water molecules that require much more energy to break than the weaker van der Waals forces between H₂S molecules
questions.explanationHtml: Water boils at 100°C; H₂S boils at −60°C — water boils far higher despite being lighter. The reason: water forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds (O–H···O) because oxygen is small, highly electronegative, and has lone pairs accessible for H-bonding. These hydrogen bonds require significant energy to break. H₂S cannot form effective hydrogen bonds (S is too large and not electronegative enough for strong H-bonding); its molecules interact only through weak van der Waals forces. This anomalously high boiling point of water compared to the other Group 16 hydrides is one of hydrogen bonding's most important consequences.
